captions.text: Because once he has the legal framework in place,
he has to physically move his assets.
And that journey is a masterpiece of suspense.
To picture this next beat, I want you to
imagine this contrast. Picture this.
Two things of different size side by side.
On one side, a massive creaking Russian
schooner, the demeanor, drifting aimlessly through thick sea
fog towards the English coast, seemingly guided
by a ghost. But on the other side,
defining that entire horrifying voyage, is a tiny
glass bottle containing a single rolledup
piece of paper. And that rolled up piece of
paper, the ship's log book, is the only administrative
record of the physical destruction of the ship.
It is the data trace of a massacre.
The voyage of the demeanor is one of the
most chilling parts of the book.
The ship leaves Varna, a port on the Black
Sea, with a cargo of silver sand and boxes
of earth. And one by one, the crew
But the captain, rather than going mad, just methodically
writes it all down in his log.
He just keeps doing his job.
Exactly. The log book becomes a ledger of death.
He writes entries like, "On 17th July,
yesterday, one of the men came to my cabin.
said that in his watch he had been sheltering
when he saw a tall, thin man who was
not like any of the crew.
It just goes on and on systematically documenting the
phantom disappearances. But what is most
crucial here is how Dracula actually travels.
He isn't flying across the ocean as a bat.
He is traveling as uninspected freight.
He's literally shipped in boxes of dirt.
